newsitem.title: UK: Knight Williams compensation fund to be freed - SIB.
newsitem.headline: Knight Williams compensation fund to be freed - SIB.

text.p: Britain's Securities and Investments Board (SIB) said on Monday it is seeking to have funds set aside by the failed UK financial adviser Knight Williams to compensate investors to be released "as soon as possible" to the sole control of the liquidators.
The SIB announcement follows a decision by the Investors Compensation Scheme (ICS) to make offers of compensation to Knights Williams investors.

Some 1.95 million pounds was set aside in April 1995 as part of the so-called "locked box" agreement between the SIB and Knight Williams. The existence and nature of the "locked box" agreement is not relevant to the amount of compensation investors can expect to receive, the SIB said.
Knight Williams, which went into voluntary liquidation in August 1995, was at the centre of the pensions mis-selling scandal after claims it gave negligent financial advice.
Knight Williams had been the country's biggest retirement income specialist managing 500 million pounds for 24,000 people before it went bust.
Pension misselling has affected several hundred thousand people who may have been wrongly advised to take out personal pensions by financial companies during the late 1980s and early 1990s.
The review into the mis-selling was launched by the SIB in 1994 but progress had been slow.
On Monday, Britain's Personal Investment Authority (PIA), which regulates the pension industry, put forward new proposals to tighten future transfers or opt-outs from occupational pension schemes.
Under the proposals all transactions related to pension transfers and opt-outs will have to be checked by a suitably qualified pensions expert.

Last week companies were given new deadlines to sort out the scandal in which as many as 1-1/2 million people may have been wrongly advised to take out personal pensions instead of staying in occupational schemes. Labour's new Treasury minister Helen Liddell also called in senior executives from the 28 worst offending firms, leaving them in no doubt that the government wanted to see progress in sorting out compensation. Liddell warned that unless it could be convinced of their sincerity, companies could face a stiffer regulatory regime under planned reform of the financial services industry.
